pos: n. (a revelatory sight granted by God to a prophet; rendering Hebrew chazon, mar'ah, Greek horama, optasia)
etymology: From Latin visio, a seeing, from videre, to see. The English word has drifted toward the man's own foresight or ambition; the biblical word is the reverse — something shown to a man who was not looking, by God who was.
biblical_def: A vision in Scripture is not a man's plan for the future but God's self-disclosure to a prophet, given while the prophet is awake and often against his expectation. The Lord defines the term Himself when Aaron and Miriam presume to speak as Moses' equals: “If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream” (Numbers 12:6). The vision is therefore a mode of revelation, ranked below the face-to-face speech granted to Moses but genuinely and objectively from God. Abram receives one: “the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision” (Genesis 15:1). Habakkuk is told to write his down and make it legible, because a vision is a message with content, not an experience with a mood: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Habakkuk 2:2). Where the word is absent, the covenant people are in famine — “the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision” (1 Samuel 3:1) — and this is the key to the most abused verse in the English Bible, Proverbs 29:18. Paul's summary of his own conversion sets the pattern for every man who has heard God speak: he was “not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” (Acts 26:19). A vision is not a thing to savour; it is a thing to obey.
webster_summary: A revelatory sight given by God to a prophet while awake. Numbers 12:6 makes it the standard prophetic mode; Habakkuk 2:2 makes it a written, legible message; Proverbs 29:18 laments its absence, not the absence of human ambition.
webster_full: VISION, n. s as z. [L. visio, from video, visus, to see.] The act of seeing external objects; actual sight.
2. The faculty of seeing; sight.
3. Something imagined to be seen, though not real; a phantom; an apparition.

4. In Scripture, a revelation from God; an appearance or exhibition of something supernaturally presented to the minds of the prophets, by which they were informed of future events. Such were the visions of Isaiah, Amos, Ezekiel.
5. Something imaginary; the production of fancy. Where there is no vision, the people perish. Prov. 29.
scriptures: Numbers 12:6
And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream.
Habakkuk 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
1 Samuel 3:1
And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.
Proverbs 29:18
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 29:18 has been lifted out of the Bible and made the motto of corporate strategy and church-growth seminars, where “vision” means the leader's ambition rather than God's revealed word — and the second half of the verse, which defines the first, is almost never quoted.
corruption_paragraphs: “Where there is no vision, the people perish” is very likely the most misappropriated half-verse in English. It is printed on leadership posters, quoted at board retreats, and preached to justify a pastor casting a five-year plan, on the assumption that vision means a compelling picture of a preferred future. The Hebrew word is chazon, the technical term for prophetic revelation — the same word that heads the books of Isaiah, Obadiah, and Nahum. The verse laments a nation with no prophetic word from God, exactly the famine described in 1 Samuel 3:1 and threatened in Amos 8:11. And Solomon supplies his own gloss in the same breath: “but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.” The antidote to no-vision is not strategic planning; it is the written law of God kept. To quote the first clause without the second is to invert the proverb into a charter for precisely the self-appointed leadership it condemns.

The second corruption is a charismatic one, and it runs in the opposite direction: the term is applied to impressions, mental pictures, and private experiences claimed as fresh revelation, with the canon left formally intact and practically supplemented. Numbers 12:6 sets vision alongside dream as the ordinary prophetic mode of the old covenant; Hebrews 1:1-2 announces that God, who spoke in those many modes, has now spoken in His Son. The dictionary holds the cessationist position of the Reformed confessions: the canon is closed, and the sufficiency of Scripture is not a claim about how much God could say but about how much He has said and bound us to. A man who has the whole written Word and still waits for a vision has not understood what he already holds in his hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazon (prophetic revelation, from chazah, to see or gaze) and mar'ah (a sight, appearance); Greek horama (that which is seen) and optasia (an appearing).
roots_lines: Hebrew chazon (H2377) — prophetic revelation, oracle; the word that titles Isaiah 1:1, Obadiah 1, and Nahum 1:1, and the word in Proverbs 29:18.
Hebrew chazah (H2372) — to gaze, behold, see as a seer; the verb behind both chazon and chozeh (seer).
Hebrew mar'ah (H4759) — a sight or appearance; the word in Numbers 12:6 and in Ezekiel's visions of God.
Greek horama (G3705) — that which is seen, a spectacle or divinely granted sight; used of Peter's sheet and Paul's Macedonian call (Acts 10:17; 16:9).
Greek optasia (G3701) — an appearing, a vision granted; used in Luke 1:22, Acts 26:19, and 2 Corinthians 12:1.
usage: “There was no open vision” — the famine of the word of God, not a shortage of leadership imagination.
“Write the vision, and make it plain” — a real vision has propositional content that can be written down and read at speed.
“Not disobedient unto the heavenly vision” — the proper response to revelation is obedience, not repetition of the experience.

pos: n. (the older Israelite title for a prophet; rendering Hebrew ro'eh and chozeh)
etymology: English agent-noun from see — one who sees. It renders two Hebrew words built on the same logic, and the KJV keeps the archaic title because Scripture itself treats it as archaic.
biblical_def: A seer is a prophet under his older name, and the Bible pauses in the middle of a narrative to tell us so: “Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer” (1 Samuel 9:9). That parenthesis is one of Scripture's few explicit lexicographical notes, and it teaches two things. First, the offices are one: the man who sees what God shows and the man who speaks what God says are the same man, because seeing is for the sake of saying. Second, the title shifted as the office matured — by the monarchy the emphasis had moved from the receiving to the proclaiming. Samuel himself answers to it plainly: “I am the seer” (1 Samuel 9:19). The chronicler lists three court seers as authors of records: “the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer” (1 Chronicles 29:29), which shows the seer as a documenting historian, not a mystic. And when Amaziah the priest of Bethel wants Amos out of the northern kingdom, he uses the title as a sneer: “O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there” (Amos 7:12) — make your living off your visions somewhere else. The state church has always preferred a prophet it pays.
webster_summary: The older Israelite title for a prophet, explained by Scripture itself in 1 Samuel 9:9. Samuel, Gad, and Nathan bore it; it carried the duty of writing records; and Amaziah threw it at Amos as an insult.
webster_full: SEER, n. [from see.] One who sees; as a seer of visions.
2. A prophet; a person who foresees future events. He that is now called a prophet, was beforetime called a seer. 1 Sam. 9.
3. One who has the gift of discerning what is hidden from ordinary sight.
4. In Scripture usage, the title borne by Samuel, Gad and Heman, denoting the recipient of divine communication.
5. Formerly applied also to the keepers of the royal chronicles, who were prophets in office.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 9:9
(Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)
1 Samuel 9:19

And Samuel answered Saul, and said, I am the seer: go up before me unto the high place; for ye shall eat with me to day, and to morrow I will let thee go, and will tell thee all that is in thine heart.
1 Chronicles 29:29
Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer,
Amos 7:12
Also Amaziah said unto Amos, O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there:
corruption_summary: The English word has been surrendered to fortune-tellers, psychics, and the occult, so that seer now suggests a crystal ball rather than a man under the word of God — and the biblical office is quietly assimilated to divination.
corruption_paragraphs: In modern usage a seer is a clairvoyant, and the drift is not innocent. It puts Samuel in the same category as the witch of Endor, whom Saul consulted precisely because Samuel was dead and God had stopped answering him (1 Samuel 28:6-7). Scripture separates the two absolutely: the seer receives what God chooses to disclose and answers to God for reporting it accurately, while the diviner seeks to extract knowledge from the unseen by technique. Deuteronomy 18:10-14 forbids the whole apparatus of observers of times, enchanters, and consulters with familiar spirits, and then in the same passage promises the true Prophet as the alternative. The office and the occult are not two grades of the same gift; they are opposites, and the shared English word hides it.

The second misuse is inside the church rather than outside it. Where the title is revived for a man said to have unusual spiritual sight, it functions to place his impressions beyond examination — the seer sees what others do not, so who can correct him? Scripture builds the correction into the office. The prophet whose word does not come to pass is to be disregarded and was not sent (Deuteronomy 18:22); the Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to test even Paul (Acts 17:11); and 1 Chronicles 29:29 shows the seers producing written records that could be checked. A man whose sight cannot be tested by the written Word is not a seer in the biblical sense whatever he is called.
roots_summary: Hebrew ro'eh (participle of ra'ah, to see) and chozeh (participle of chazah, to gaze); both mean one who sees, and 1 Samuel 9:9 glosses them by the later term nabi, prophet.
roots_lines: Hebrew ro'eh (H7200 participle) — one seeing; the archaic title in 1 Samuel 9:9, 11, 18-19, used of Samuel.
Hebrew chozeh (H2374) — a gazer, beholder; the title of Gad (2 Samuel 24:11) and Amos's title in Amos 7:12.
Hebrew nabi (H5030) — prophet, spokesman; the later and dominant title, which 1 Samuel 9:9 says replaced ro'eh.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, look, perceive; the ordinary verb of sight, which is why the title is not mystical but plain.
Greek has no exact equivalent title; the Septuagint renders both Hebrew terms by ho blepon (the one seeing) or simply prophetes.
usage: “He that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer” — Scripture's own note that the two titles name one office.
“I am the seer” — Samuel identifies himself plainly, without mystique.
“O thou seer, go, flee thee away” — the establishment's standing offer to the true prophet: prophesy elsewhere, and eat there.

etymology: Old English beorhtnes, from beorht, shining, clear. In Scripture the word is almost always theological: it names the visible outshining of the glory of God, and in Hebrews it names the Son's relation to the Father.
biblical_def: Brightness is the shining-forth of glory, and the New Testament uses it to state one of the most precise Christological claims in Scripture: the Son is “the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person” (Hebrews 1:3). The Greek is apaugasma, the radiance that streams from a light source — not a lamp lit from another lamp, which would be a second and later thing, but the shining that is coeval with and inseparable from the light itself. This is the language the Nicene fathers reached for in light of light, very God of very God, and it is why eternal generation is not a speculation but an exegesis: a light is never without its radiance. In the Old Testament the word attends the appearances of God. Ezekiel, groping for words at the end of his vision, says “so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” (Ezekiel 1:28) — and falls on his face. Isaiah makes it eschatological and missionary at once: “the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising” (Isaiah 60:3). And Paul makes it the instrument of judgment: the man of sin is destroyed “with the brightness of his coming” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The same radiance that draws the nations annihilates the antichrist; brightness saves and brightness kills, depending on what it falls upon.
webster_summary: The outshining of glory. Hebrews 1:3 makes it the technical term for the Son's eternal relation to the Father; Ezekiel falls on his face before it; Isaiah says kings will come to it; Paul says it destroys the Wicked one.
webster_full: BRIGHTNESS, n. [See Bright.] Splendor; luster; glitter; as the brightness of the sun.
2. Acuteness, applied to the faculties; sharpness of wit; as the brightness of a man's parts.
3. In Scripture, the visible effulgence attending the manifested glory of God; as the brightness of his rising. Is. 60.
4. That which shines forth from a luminous body, inseparable from the body itself.
5. Clearness; freedom from obscurity or dimness.
scriptures: Hebrews 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
Ezekiel 1:28

As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake.
Isaiah 60:3
And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising.
2 Thessalonians 2:8
And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming:
corruption_summary: Hebrews 1:3 is read as a poetic compliment rather than a metaphysical statement, and the eternal generation of the Son that it teaches is treated as optional speculation — leaving the door open to the subordinationism the word was chosen to shut.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole force of apaugasma is that radiance is not made, not adopted, and not later. Arius taught that there was when the Son was not; the writer of Hebrews had already answered him by three centuries with a metaphor that cannot be pried apart. You cannot have the glory without the brightness, nor date the brightness after the glory. When modern treatments soften this into imagery about Jesus reflecting God's character, the metaphor is quietly reversed — a reflection is a separate surface receiving borrowed light, which is precisely what apaugasma denies. The dictionary holds the Nicene and confessional position without hedging: the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, of one substance with Him, and Hebrews 1:3 is one of the load-bearing texts.

A second and lesser drift affects Isaiah 60:3 and 2 Thessalonians 2:8, which are frequently split apart as though brightness were a merely comforting category. Scripture will not allow the separation. The nations walk to the brightness and the antichrist is consumed by it in the same divine outshining, exactly as the pillar of fire lit Israel and troubled the Egyptians in one night (Exodus 14:20). The light does not change; the relation to it does. Any account of God's glory that can only warm and never wound has taken half a Bible.
roots_summary: Hebrew nogahh (shining, radiance) and zohar (brilliance); Greek apaugasma (effulgence streaming from a source) and epiphaneia (appearing, manifestation).
roots_lines: Hebrew nogahh (H5051) — brightness, shining; used of the LORD's theophanic light in 2 Samuel 22:13 and Ezekiel 1:28.
Hebrew zohar (H2096) — brilliance, splendour; used in Daniel 12:3 of the wise shining as the brightness of the firmament.
Greek apaugasma (G541) — effulgence, radiance issuing from a light source; the hapax of Hebrews 1:3.
Greek epiphaneia (G2015) — appearing, manifestation; the word rendered brightness in 2 Thessalonians 2:8 and elsewhere appearing.
Greek charakter (G5481) — the exact impress of a die, the companion term in Hebrews 1:3 rendered express image.
usage: “The brightness of his glory” — not a reflection of God but the outshining of God, inseparable from the source.
“Kings to the brightness of thy rising” — the missionary pull of God's glory shining on His people.
“Destroy with the brightness of his coming” — the same radiance is the end of the man of sin.

pos: v.t. (to cry aloud publicly with authority; rendering Hebrew qara, Greek kerusso)
etymology: From Latin proclamare, to cry out — pro, forth, and clamare, to shout. The Latin keeps the herald's posture: a proclamation is not an argument offered but a decree announced by a man who did not write it.
biblical_def: To proclaim is to publish a decree on someone else's authority, and the first and greatest instance has God as the herald of His own name: “I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious” (Exodus 33:19). Everything the herald's office means is there — the content is God's character, the timing is God's choosing, and the sovereignty of the mercy is stated in the same sentence, which is why Paul quotes precisely this verse in Romans 9:15 to establish unconditional election. The word then governs the calendar: Israel's feasts are not customs that arose but convocations she is commanded to announce, “the feasts of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations” (Leviticus 23:2). It governs the economy: in the jubilee year Israel must “proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” (Leviticus 25:10), the verse cast on the Liberty Bell. And it governs the Messiah's ministry, where the jubilee language returns as gospel: the Anointed is sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isaiah 61:1), the text the Lord read at Nazareth and closed the book upon. Preaching in the New Testament is kerusso, this same herald's work: not persuasion, discussion, or exploration, but the public announcement of a finished decree.
webster_summary: To announce publicly on another's authority. God proclaims His own name to Moses; Israel proclaims the feasts and the jubilee liberty; and the Messiah is sent to proclaim liberty to captives — the pattern behind New Testament preaching.
webster_full: PROCLAIM, v.t. [L. proclamo; pro and clamo, to cry out.] To promulgate; to announce; to publish; as, to proclaim a fast.
2. To denounce; to give official notice of.
3. To declare with honor; as, to proclaim the name of the Lord. Ex. 33.
4. To outlaw by public denunciation.
PROCLAMATION, n. The act of announcing or publishing by authority; official notice given to the public.
scriptures: Exodus 33:19

And he said, I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy.
Leviticus 23:2
Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, Concerning the feasts of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations, even these are my feasts.
Leviticus 25:10

And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
Isaiah 61:1

The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
corruption_summary: Preaching has been redefined from proclamation into conversation — the herald replaced by the facilitator, the decree replaced by the shared exploration — and the shift is defended as humility when it is in fact a change of office.
corruption_paragraphs: A herald has no authority over his message and no permission to soften it; that is the whole point of the office, and it is why Scripture chose the word. When preaching is recast as dialogue, story-sharing, or a journey undertaken alongside the hearers, the man in the pulpit has silently exchanged the herald's commission for the moderator's. The change is usually presented as a virtue — who am I to declare? — but Scripture treats the reluctance as disobedience, not modesty. Paul's charge is to “preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” and to do it as one who knows that men will not endure sound doctrine (2 Timothy 4:2-3). A herald who takes a vote on the decree has not humbled himself; he has deserted his post.

The jubilee texts are corrupted in a second direction, by being read as a political programme detached from their covenantal frame. Leviticus 25 proclaims liberty because the land belongs to the LORD and Israel are His tenants, and the release is tied to atonement — the jubilee is announced on the day of atonement itself (Leviticus 25:9). Isaiah 61:1 takes that machinery and applies it to the release of sinners, which is exactly how the Lord Jesus applied it in the synagogue at Nazareth. To lift the language of proclaimed liberty out of that setting and make it a slogan for economic redistribution keeps the vocabulary and discards the atonement that funds it.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara (to call, cry, proclaim) and shama in the causative (to cause to be heard); Greek kerusso (to herald) and katangello (to announce down to).
roots_lines: Hebrew qara (H7121) — to call out, cry, proclaim; the verb in Exodus 33:19, Leviticus 23:2, Leviticus 25:10, and Isaiah 61:1.
Hebrew deror (H1865) — liberty, a flowing free; the noun proclaimed in Leviticus 25:10 and Isaiah 61:1.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to publish a decree as a public crier; the standard New Testament word for preaching.
Greek keryx (G2783) — the herald himself; Paul calls himself one in 1 Timothy 2:7 and 2 Timothy 1:11.
Greek katangello (G2605) — to announce, declare thoroughly; used of proclaiming the Lord's death in 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee” — God is the first herald of His own character, and He sets the terms of the mercy in the same breath.
“Proclaim liberty throughout all the land” — the jubilee release, announced on the day of atonement.
“To proclaim liberty to the captives” — the jubilee taken up as the gospel and read by Christ at Nazareth.

pos: v.i. (to wander from the truth or the way; rendering Hebrew ta'ah, shagah, Greek planao)
etymology: From Latin errare, to wander, stray, rove — the same root that gives errant and erratic. The Latin is spatial before it is intellectual, and so is the Hebrew: to err is first to go off the road, and only then to be wrong.
biblical_def: To err in Scripture is to wander off the way, and the physical image governs the moral one throughout. The Lord's verdict on the wilderness generation is not that they miscalculated but that they strayed: “It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways” (Psalm 95:10, quoted in Hebrews 3:10). Two things are joined there — erring is located in the heart, not merely the head, and its consequence is ignorance of God's ways, His roads. The Psalter is explicit that the standard which defines wandering is the written law: “Thou hast rebuked the proud that are cursed, which do err from thy commandments” (Psalm 119:21). Isaiah shows the leadership erring first and the people after: “the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink… they err in vision, they stumble in judgment” (Isaiah 28:7) — a drunken clergy still holding office, still issuing oracles, and getting them wrong. The Lord Jesus states the cause with a diagnostic precision that closes the matter: “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God” (Matthew 22:29). Error has two ordinary sources, and both are named — ignorance of what God has said, and underestimation of what God can do. The Sadducees had the whole Bible and still fell into both.
webster_summary: To wander from the way, first physically and then morally. The wilderness generation erred in heart; the priest and prophet erred in vision through drink; and Christ traces all error to ignorance of the Scriptures and of the power of God.
webster_full: ERR, v.i. [L. erro; Fr. errer; It. errare; Sp. errar; to wander.] To wander from the right way; to deviate from the true course or purpose.
2. To miss the right way, in morals or religion; to deviate from the path or line of duty; to stray by design or mistake.
3. To mistake; to commit error; to take or hold a wrong opinion. Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures. Matt. 22.
4. To wander; to ramble; to rove.
ERROR, n. A wandering or deviation from the truth; a mistake in judgment, by which men assent to what is not true.
scriptures: Matthew 22:29
Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.
Psalm 95:10
Forty years long was I grieved with this generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways:
Psalm 119:21
Thou hast rebuked the proud that are cursed, which do err from thy commandments.
Isaiah 28:7

But they also have erred through wine, and through strong drink are out of the way; the priest and the prophet have erred through strong drink, they are swallowed up of wine, they are out of the way through strong drink; they err in vision, they stumble in judgment.
corruption_summary: Error has been reclassified from a moral wandering into an honest difference of perspective, so that the category of being wrong about God quietly disappears — and with it the duty to recover the one who errs.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to treat doctrinal error as a matter of interpretation, on which sincere readers land differently and no one is culpable. Scripture does not know this category. Psalm 119:21 calls those who err from the commandments proud and cursed; Matthew 22:29 tells the Sadducees flatly that they are wrong and names the reason; and James ends his epistle with the duty this creates: if any do err from the truth and one convert him, he has saved a soul from death and hidden a multitude of sins (James 5:19-20). Error is a road leading somewhere, and the man on it can be turned around. Relabelling it perspective removes the danger and abolishes the rescue in the same motion.

Isaiah 28:7 addresses the second corruption, which is inside the ministry rather than outside it. The priest and the prophet in that verse have not left their posts; they are erring in vision and stumbling in judgment while still functioning. A church that examines its members but never its teachers has read only half the prophets. The Reformed insistence on confessional subscription, presbyteries and associations, and the public examination of ordinands is not institutional suspicion; it is obedience to a text that expects the men in office to be the ones who wander first.
roots_summary: Hebrew ta'ah (to wander, stray, as sheep) and shagah (to go astray, err inadvertently); Greek planao (to cause to wander, deceive), the root of planet, the wandering star.
roots_lines: Hebrew ta'ah (H8582) — to wander, go astray; used of sheep, of drunkards, and of Israel wandering from the LORD.
Hebrew shagah (H7686) — to stray, err, especially through inadvertence or intoxication; the verb in Isaiah 28:7.
Greek planao (G4105) — to lead astray, cause to wander; passive, to be deceived; the verb in Matthew 22:29.
Greek plane (G4106) — the wandering itself, error; used of the error of Balaam (Jude 11) and of the wicked (2 Peter 3:17).
Latin errare — to wander; the source of English err, error, errant, and erratic, all keeping the road metaphor.
usage: “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God” — the two standing causes of religious error, named by Christ.
“They do err in their heart” — error is seated in the affections before it appears in the opinions.
“They err in vision, they stumble in judgment” — men still in office and still prophesying, and wrong.

pos: adv. (out of the right way, wandering; rendering Hebrew ta'ah, Greek planao)
etymology: From Middle English astraied, out of Old French estraier, to stray or roam — ultimately the same Latin strata, the paved road, that gives street. To go astray is literally to leave the road.
biblical_def: Astray is the Bible's picture of sin as sheep-behaviour, and Isaiah 53:6 compresses the whole doctrine of human ruin and divine substitution into one verse: “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all”. Three clauses, three doctrines. All we — the ruin is universal, with no remnant of the self-directed. Every one to his own way — the ruin is individual and willed, not a herd accident; sheep do not stray in formation, each takes its own line, and the sinner's own way is precisely the problem. The LORD hath laid on him — the remedy is not the sheep's return but the Father's act of imputation upon another. Peter takes up the same figure for the converted: “ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). The Lord Jesus makes it a parable of seeking love: the shepherd leaves the ninety and nine “and seeketh that which is gone astray” (Matthew 18:12). And the psalmist supplies the believer's honest testimony in both tenses — “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments” (Psalm 119:176). He knows the commandments and has still wandered, which is why he asks to be sought rather than promising to return.
webster_summary: Out of the right way, as a straying sheep. Isaiah 53:6 makes it the universal and individual account of sin, answered by the LORD laying our iniquity on the Substitute; Peter and Christ apply the figure to conversion and to seeking love.
webster_full: ASTRAY, adv. [a and stray. See Stray.] Out of the right way or proper place, both in a literal and figurative sense.
2. In morals or religion, wandering from the path of rectitude, from duty and happiness. Before I was afflicted I went astray. Ps. 119.
3. Applied to cattle and sheep, escaped from enclosure and roaming at large.
4. To go astray, to leave the flock or the road; hence, to sin.
5. Lost; missing; not in the appointed place.
scriptures: Isaiah 53:6
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
1 Peter 2:25
For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.
Matthew 18:12
How think ye? if a man have an hundred sheep, and one of them be gone astray, doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray?
Psalm 119:176
I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments.
corruption_summary: The sheep image is sentimentalised into helpless innocence — the poor lost lamb who is merely misplaced rather than rebellious — which deletes the middle clause of Isaiah 53:6, where every one turns to his own way.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular treatments of the lost sheep make the animal the object of pity and nothing else: it did not mean to wander, it simply got lost, and the shepherd's love is the whole story. Isaiah will not permit the reading. Between the straying and the substitution stands the clause “we have turned every one to his own way” — deliberate, self-directed, and individual. That is total depravity stated in the vocabulary of animal husbandry, and it is why the sheep cannot be its own remedy. The comfort of the passage is not that the sheep was innocent but that the iniquity was real and was laid on someone else. Remove the guilt and the substitution becomes decorative.

The opposite corruption is a hardness that reads Matthew 18:12 as though the ninety and nine were the point — the safe majority whose security matters more than the one. The Lord's own application forbids it: it is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish (Matthew 18:14). Both errors come from taking the picture without the doctrine. The strayed sheep is guilty and is sought; a shepherd who denied the first would be sentimental, and one who denied the second would not be a shepherd.
roots_summary: Hebrew ta'ah (to wander, as sheep or drunkards) and shagah; Greek planao, the verb of wandering that gives planet; the underlying picture in every language is livestock off the road.
roots_lines: Hebrew ta'ah (H8582) — to wander, stray, go astray; the verb in Isaiah 53:6 and Psalm 119:176.
Hebrew 'abad (H6) — to perish, be lost; the word behind lost sheep in Psalm 119:176 and Jeremiah 50:6.
Greek planao (G4105) — to lead astray; in the passive, to wander; used in 1 Peter 2:25 and Matthew 18:12.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; the title Peter joins to Shepherd in 1 Peter 2:25 for the One the strayed return to.
Old French estraier, from Latin strata (paved road) — the English word keeps the road that was left.
usage: “All we like sheep have gone astray” — universal ruin, stated in one clause.
“We have turned every one to his own way” — the straying is willed and individual, not accidental.
“Seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments” — the believer who has wandered asks to be sought, not merely to be pardoned.

pos: adj. (full of deceit, treacherous, misleading; rendering Hebrew mirmah, 'aqob, Greek dolios)
etymology: From Old French deceite, past participle of decevoir, from Latin decipere — de, away, and capere, to take. To deceive is to catch a man away, as with a snare; the deceitful thing is the bait that works.
biblical_def: Deceitful in Scripture is applied first and most devastatingly not to enemies but to the reader's own heart: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). The Hebrew 'aqob is built on the root behind Jacob the supplanter — the heart is a heel-grabber, and the superlative above all things means it out-deceives every external deceiver a man will ever meet. The question that closes the verse is not rhetorical despair but a set-up: the next verse answers it — “I the LORD search the heart” (Jeremiah 17:10). The word then covers three familiar frauds. It covers the tongue: “Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 120:2). It covers false ministry, where Paul strips the disguise off men who look most like the real thing — “false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:13); the danger is precisely that they are transformed into the likeness, not away from it. And it covers the world's most universally trusted evidence, physical beauty: “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). The three together make the point that deceit is not chiefly a matter of stated falsehoods but of reliable-looking things that will not bear weight.
webster_summary: Full of deceit, misleading in appearance. Jeremiah applies it to the reader's own heart above all things; Paul to false apostles who transform themselves into the real thing; Solomon to beauty and favour, which promise what they cannot pay.
webster_full: DECEITFUL, a. Tending to mislead, deceive or ensnare; as deceitful practices.
2. Full of deceit; trickish; fraudulent; cheating; as a deceitful man.
3. Deceptive; delusive; not answering the appearance or expectation; as a deceitful proof; deceitful weights. Prov. 11.
4. Insincere; hollow; as deceitful professions of friendship.
DECEIT, n. The misleading of a person; the leading of another person to believe what is false, or not to believe what is true.
scriptures: Jeremiah 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Proverbs 31:30
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
2 Corinthians 11:13
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
Psalm 120:2
Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue.
corruption_summary: “Follow your heart” is the exact inversion of Jeremiah 17:9, and it has become the settled moral counsel of the age — including inside the church, where it is preached as authenticity.
corruption_paragraphs: No sentence in modern moral instruction is repeated more often, or contradicts Scripture more precisely, than the counsel to trust your heart. Jeremiah says the heart is the most deceitful thing there is, out-deceiving every liar and every false teacher a man will encounter, and that no man can even audit his own. Solomon says the same in the imperative: “He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool” (Proverbs 28:26). The counsel is not that the heart's desires are always wrong — it is that the heart is an unreliable witness about itself, and therefore cannot be the court of appeal for its own case. The remedy Scripture gives is external: the searching of God (Jeremiah 17:10), the written Word which discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart (Hebrews 4:12), and a new heart given in regeneration (Ezekiel 36:26). Authenticity as a virtue asks the accused to preside at his own trial.

Proverbs 31:30 is corrupted in two opposite ways and neither reads the verse. It is used to disparage beauty as though the text called it evil; it says vain, meaning it does not last and cannot bear the weight put on it, which is a statement about durability rather than morality. And it is quietly dropped altogether by a culture that has organised its entire commercial apparatus around favour and appearance. Solomon's contrast is the point: the fear of the LORD is the one quality in the chapter that will still be praised when the face has gone, and it is the only one he tells the reader to praise.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'aqob (crooked, supplanting — the root of Jacob's name) and mirmah (fraud, treachery); Greek dolios (crafty, from dolos, a bait or snare).
roots_lines: Hebrew 'aqob (H6121) — deceitful, crooked, from 'aqab, to take by the heel, supplant; the word in Jeremiah 17:9.
Hebrew mirmah (H4820) — deceit, fraud, treachery; used of false balances and of a guileful tongue.
Hebrew remiyyah (H7423) — slackness, deceit; used of a deceitful bow in Psalm 78:57.
Greek dolios (G1386) — deceitful, crafty; from dolos, originally a bait for fish, then any trick; the word in 2 Corinthians 11:13.
Greek apate (G539) — deceitfulness, delusion; the deceitfulness of riches (Matthew 13:22) and of sin (Hebrews 3:13).
usage: “The heart is deceitful above all things” — the standing warning against self-trust, and the reason the counsel to follow your heart is exactly backwards.
“Deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ” — false ministry succeeds by resemblance, not by difference.
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain” — not that they are evil, but that they will not bear the weight laid on them.

pos: adv. (untruly, with intent to deceive; rendering Hebrew sheqer used adverbially, Greek pseudomenoi)
etymology: From Latin falsus, past participle of fallere, to deceive. The adverb is the legal form of the word: it describes not a mistaken statement but a statement made against known truth, usually under oath or against a neighbour.
biblical_def: Falsely is a courtroom and covenant word. Its home is the ninth commandment and the law of oaths, where Leviticus states the two prohibitions together: “Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another” (Leviticus 19:11), and then raises the stakes by attaching the Name: “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:12). A false oath is not merely a lie told to a man; it is a profanation, because it calls God as witness to a thing God knows to be untrue. Jeremiah finds a whole religious economy built on the practice and traces the corruption from the top down and the bottom up at once: “The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so: and what will ye do in the end thereof?” (Jeremiah 5:31). The clergy lie, the priests profit by it, and the people prefer it — a false ministry always has a constituency. The Lord Jesus then turns the word around and makes it a beatitude: the disciples are blessed when men “shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Matthew 5:11), with the qualifier falsely doing essential work, since there is no blessing on reproach a man has earned. Paul applies the adverb to a whole discipline: “oppositions of science falsely so called” (1 Timothy 6:20) — knowledge wearing the name of knowledge.
webster_summary: Untruly, against known truth. Leviticus binds it to the Name in the law of oaths; Jeremiah shows a whole priesthood profiting by it while the people prefer it; Christ blesses only reproach that is false; Paul names knowledge falsely so called.
webster_full: FALSELY, adv. In a manner contrary to truth and fact; not truly; erroneously.
2. Treacherously; perfidiously. He falsely betrayed his trust.
3. Insincerely; not honestly; as, he falsely professed friendship.
4. Contrary to the true and proper sense of the term; as, science falsely so called. 1 Tim. 6.
FALSE, a. [L. falsus, from fallo, to deceive.] Not true; not conformable to fact; expressing what is contrary to that which exists, is done, said or thought.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:11
Ye shall not steal, neither deal falsely, neither lie one to another.
Leviticus 19:12
And ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God: I am the LORD.
Jeremiah 5:31
The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so: and what will ye do in the end thereof?
Matthew 5:11
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
corruption_summary: The qualifier is dropped from Matthew 5:11, so that opposition of any kind is claimed as persecution for Christ's sake — and 1 Timothy 6:20 is meanwhile used to dismiss real knowledge rather than the counterfeit Paul actually named.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 5:11 contains a word that is almost always omitted when the verse is claimed: falsely, and with it the phrase for my sake. The Lord blesses those slandered by lies on His account. He does not bless the man whose obnoxiousness has earned him the criticism he receives, and Peter draws the line explicitly — let none suffer as a busybody in other men's matters, but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed (1 Peter 4:15-16). The habit of treating every rebuke as evidence of faithfulness is an effective way to become unteachable, and it borrows the language of martyrdom to do it. The test is simple and is written in the text: is the accusation false, and is it on account of Christ?

Paul's phrase in 1 Timothy 6:20 is likewise abused. Science falsely so called is the Greek pseudonymos gnosis — knowledge wearing a name that does not belong to it, aimed at the incipient gnosticism troubling Ephesus. It is not a blanket verdict on natural philosophy, which Scripture elsewhere commends by sending the sluggard to the ant and by having Solomon catalogue trees and beasts (Proverbs 6:6; 1 Kings 4:33). The verse condemns a specific counterfeit: a body of speculative teaching claiming the prestige of knowledge while contradicting the deposit entrusted to Timothy. Used as a slogan against learning as such, it becomes an excuse for the ignorance Christ named as a cause of error in Matthew 22:29.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheqer (falsehood, deception, used adverbially in the oath texts) and kachash (to deny, deal falsely); Greek pseudomai (to lie) and the prefix pseudo- in pseudonymos.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, lie, deception; the word in Leviticus 19:12 and in Jeremiah's indictments of the prophets.
Hebrew kachash (H3584) — to lie, deceive, deal falsely; the verb in Leviticus 19:11.
Greek pseudomai (G5574) — to speak falsely, lie; the participle in Matthew 5:11.
Greek pseudonymos (G5581) — falsely named; the hapax in 1 Timothy 6:20, rendered falsely so called.
Greek gnosis (G1108) — knowledge; the noun that the false name is attached to, and the term the gnostics later claimed.
usage: “Ye shall not swear by my name falsely” — a false oath profanes the Name it invokes.
“My people love to have it so” — false prophecy is a market with willing buyers.
“All manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” — the two qualifiers that define the blessing.

pos: adv. (faithlessly, in violation of covenant; rendering the Hebrew verb bagad)
etymology: From Old French trecherie, trickery, from trechier, to cheat. In the KJV it almost always renders one Hebrew verb, bagad, whose noun means a garment — the treacherous man covers himself, and Malachi plays on exactly that image.
biblical_def: To deal treacherously is to break faith with one to whom you were bound, and the word belongs to covenant rather than to ordinary dishonesty. Its densest use is Malachi's indictment of easy divorce, where the prophet answers a congregation that cannot understand why God ignores its offerings: “the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant” (Malachi 2:14). Marriage is here a covenant with God as witness, which is why its breach is treachery and not merely unkindness; and the chapter closes with a warning aimed at the inner man: “take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” (Malachi 2:16). The same verb makes marital unfaithfulness the model for Israel's idolatry: “Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 3:20). And Isaiah piles the root on itself in a cry of exhaustion at a world where faithlessness has become the norm — “the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously” (Isaiah 24:16). The repetition is the point. Treachery is the sin that destroys the possibility of any other dealing, because it attacks the trust every other transaction stands on.
webster_summary: Faithlessly, in breach of covenant. Malachi makes it the verdict on divorce, with God as witness to the marriage; Jeremiah makes marital treachery the pattern of idolatry; Isaiah repeats the root four times in a single verse of grief.
webster_full: TREACHEROUSLY, adv. By violating allegiance or faith pledged; by betraying a trust; faithlessly; perfidiously.
2. In a manner to betray; as, he dealt treacherously with his companion.
TREACHEROUS, a. [Fr. trecheur, a cheat.] Violating allegiance or faith pledged; false; faithless.
3. Betraying or discovering a trust reposed; as a treacherous friend.
4. In Scripture, applied to breach of the marriage covenant and of covenant with God. Mal. 2.
scriptures: Malachi 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
Malachi 2:16

For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously.
Jeremiah 3:20
Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.
Isaiah 24:16

From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously.
corruption_summary: Malachi 2:16 is softened or re-punctuated until it no longer says that God hates putting away, and the covenant frame that makes divorce treachery rather than misfortune is replaced by the language of two people growing apart.
corruption_paragraphs: The plain sense of Malachi 2:16 in the Authorized Version is that the LORD hates putting away — hates the act of divorce — and the surrounding verses supply the reason: He was the witness at the wedding, and He counts its dissolution a breach of covenant against a companion. That has proved an unwelcome verse, and a good deal of ingenuity has been spent on making it say something else, most often by recasting it as a condemnation only of the man who divorces treacherously rather than of putting away as such. The dictionary keeps the received text and reads Malachi with the Lord Jesus, who takes the same ground in Matthew 19:4-9: from the beginning it was not so, what God has joined man is not to sunder, and the single exception granted is for fornication. That is neither the absolute prohibition of Rome nor the elastic permission of the age.

Underneath the exegetical dispute lies a change of category that costs more. When a marriage ends, modern speech supplies vocabulary in which no one has done anything: the relationship ran its course, the parties grew apart, it was no longer fulfilling. Bagad names an agent and a victim — someone dealt treacherously, and someone was dealt with. Malachi's congregation was genuinely baffled by God's displeasure and asked wherefore?, which is exactly the response the covenant frame produces when it has been forgotten. The recovery is not a harsher tone toward the divorced, many of whom were the ones betrayed, but the restoration of the frame: marriage is a covenant sworn before a Witness who does not forget the terms.
roots_summary: Hebrew bagad (to act covertly, deal treacherously, break faith), related to beged, a garment or covering — the treacherous man conceals himself, and Malachi 2:16 turns the pun on covering violence with a garment.
roots_lines: Hebrew bagad (H898) — to act treacherously, deal faithlessly; the verb in Malachi 2:14-16, Jeremiah 3:20, and Isaiah 24:16.
Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment, covering; the cognate noun, and the image behind covering violence with a garment.
Hebrew bogedim — the treacherous dealers; the participle repeated for effect in Isaiah 24:16 and Jeremiah 12:1.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the bond whose breach makes the dealing treacherous rather than merely unkind.
Greek asynthetos (G802) — covenant-breakers; the Septuagint and Pauline equivalent, listed in Romans 1:31.
usage: “The wife of thy covenant” — the phrase that makes divorce a covenant breach and not a private disappointment.
“Take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” — the guard is set on the inner man before the act.
“The treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously” — Isaiah's cry at a society where faithlessness has become ordinary.

pos: adj. (out of one's mind, insane; also, enraged; rendering Hebrew shaga, halal, Greek mainomai)
etymology: Old English gemaed, out of one's mind. The KJV always uses it of madness proper, never in the modern colloquial sense of merely angry — a shift in English that now costs the reader several verses.
biblical_def: Mad in the Authorized Version means insane, and three of its uses are essential to reading the Bible's account of how the world judges the faithful. David, cornered in Gath, saves his life by counterfeiting insanity: he “changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1 Samuel 21:13). The anointed king of Israel drooling on a Philistine gatepost is one of Scripture's starkest pictures of the interval between promise and throne. The Lord Jesus receives the charge in earnest: “He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” (John 10:20) — the crowd's argument is not that His teaching is false but that a madman need not be answered, which remains the most economical way to dismiss anyone. Paul receives it too, from a Roman governor who is impressed rather than hostile: “Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad” (Acts 26:24). His reply is a model of Christian composure under the charge of fanaticism: “I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness” (Acts 26:25). He neither rages nor retreats; he claims the two things Festus had denied him, truth and sobriety. Ecclesiastes adds the sober warning that madness can be inflicted: “oppression maketh a wise man mad” (Ecclesiastes 7:7).
webster_summary: Insane, out of one's mind — never the modern sense of merely angry. David feigned it to escape Gath; the crowd used it to dismiss Christ without answering Him; Festus threw it at Paul, who answered with truth and soberness.
webster_full: MAD, a. [Sax. gemaad, mad.] Disordered in intellect; distracted; furious.
2. Proceeding from disordered intellect; as mad demeanor.
3. Enraged; furious; as, the people were mad against him.
4. Infatuated with folly. The nations are mad upon their idols. Jer. 50.
5. Distracted with anxiety or trouble; as, oppression maketh a wise man mad. Eccl. 7.
scriptures: Acts 26:24
And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
Acts 26:25
But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
John 10:20
And many of them said, He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?
1 Samuel 21:13
And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard.
corruption_summary: The archaism trips modern readers into hearing angry where the text says insane; and the ancient tactic in John 10:20 — declaring a man deranged so that his argument need not be met — has been rebuilt as a diagnostic vocabulary and turned on Christians who hold the historic faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The lexical problem is small and worth naming: in current English mad ordinarily means angry, and a reader who carries that sense into Acts 26:24 will miss that Festus was questioning Paul's sanity, not his temper. Every KJV use is the older and stronger sense — deranged, out of one's mind — and Paul's answer confirms it, since he offers soberness as the opposite, which is the antonym of insanity rather than of anger. Reading the archaism correctly restores what the exchange actually was: a courteous, high-stakes dispute about whether a rational man could believe in a resurrection.

The tactic in John 10:20 is the durable corruption, and it has never been improved upon: why hear ye him? If a man can be classified as disordered, his claims need never be examined. The twentieth century industrialised this in the punitive psychiatry of the Soviet state, where dissent was itself the diagnosis; the present form is softer and more diffuse, reaching for the language of phobia, pathology, and harm to place a Christian conviction outside the range of things that can be argued with. The dictionary names the move for what it is, an evasion of the argument rather than an answer to it, and takes Paul's reply as the model — not indignation, but the calm insistence that what is being said is true and sober, and can be examined by anyone willing to look at the evidence he had just laid out.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaga (to rave, be mad) and halal in one stem (to be boastful, then foolish, then mad); Greek mainomai (to rave) and the milder existemi (to be beside oneself).
roots_lines: Hebrew shaga (H7696) — to rave, act like a madman; the verb in 1 Samuel 21:13-15 and 2 Kings 9:11.
Hebrew halal (H1984) — in the poel stem, to be foolish or mad; distinct in sense from the same root meaning to praise.
Greek mainomai (G3105) — to be mad, rave; used in John 10:20, Acts 12:15, Acts 26:24-25, and 1 Corinthians 14:23.
Greek existemi (G1839) — to be beside oneself, amazed; used of the charge against Christ in Mark 3:21 and by Festus in Acts 26:24.
Greek sophrosyne (G4997) — soundness of mind, soberness; the exact word Paul opposes to madness in Acts 26:25.
usage: “I am not mad, most noble Festus” — the model answer to the charge of fanaticism: courteous, and claiming truth and soberness.
“He hath a devil, and is mad; why hear ye him?” — the oldest way to avoid answering an argument.
“Oppression maketh a wise man mad” — Ecclesiastes on what sustained injustice does to a sound mind.
